body: scripts/issues::mark_read: where the reading person has no ledger yet, mark_read seeds a fresh ledger (every live and archived record at its current agent mark) under the same lock before raising the record's mark, so the first read of a record that existed before the ledger reports 0 marked, as the seed rule counts it read

scripts/issues::read_ledger: a ledger file that is not a JSON object whose records map '<id> <opened>' to {first_read (a time), mark (an integer)} refuses with reason invalid on every reader and on read (CLI exit 2, dashboard 409); the message names the file and says deleting it starts a fresh ledger with everything counted read
scripts/issues::mark_read writes the ledger only when the entry is new, the mark rises, or the ledger is being seeded; a repeat read writes nothing

.ok-planner/review/project.md:32 says 'read <id> [--opened <time>] marks every agent message read'; after this stage it records the read in the caller's git-ignored ledger and refuses with no name. The inputs are unchanged, so this stage left the entry; the issue-format item that edits project.md should restate it

artifact-definitions.md:244 defines unread as 'agent messages the owner has not yet read' and :253 gives a reply's read field as 'null until the owner reads it'; after this stage unread and unopened come from the reading person's ledger and new agent messages carry no read field (retired, accepted when present). The issue-format item that edits this file should restate both

body: scripts/ports loads the issues module through load_sibling (as scripts/review does) and takes tasks from issues.tasks, so the registry write imports issues.write_records (mkstemp in the cache folder, then os.replace) instead of copying it; root and cache come from tasks.project_root() and tasks.cache_dir(). Rule 6.

ports lease/release run outside any estate exit 2 with 'tasks: no project estate ...', the refusal tasks.project_root() owns, not the 1 the notes give for refusals; every refusal ports itself makes exits 1.

PORTS.RUN.FAILED carries error, message, trace, and a fixed registry field (.ok-planner/.cache/ports.json), so a registry that does not parse is named in the event without a converting catch; a registry whose leases or ports are not objects fails an assertion that names the path.

The bind probe's catch emits PORTS.PORT.HELD (port, address, errno, trace) for each refused bind and returns held; an absent IPv6 stack is detected once per call (bind of :: port 0) and emits PORTS.IPV6.ABSENT, after which only 0.0.0.0 and 127.0.0.1 are probed; any other OSError propagates. Per the events standard, a caught error emits.

ports check-range prints one line, 'port_range F-L holds N port(s); K are on the block list (<port> <what>, ...), so N-K remain to lease' (or 'none is on the block list'), counting block-list hits only, not ports held at that moment; it refuses on stderr as 'ports: <reason>', which the core's range_refusal relays by that prefix. The reach refusal reads 'port_range F-L reaches the machine's ephemeral range, which starts at N'; lease appends '; choose a range below N through /ok'.

ports suggest-range lists every 200-port window from 1025 up to the ephemeral start that the block list does not touch, shuffles them with SystemRandom, and prints the first window none of whose ports is held now as FIRST-LAST; it refuses when no window qualifies. On this macOS host /etc/services leaves 65 gaps of at least 200 ports.
The lease cursor 'next' is one past the highest port the lease took, wrapping to first when that port is the range's last.
ports lease checks the names before the range, so a project that declares neither is told to declare the names and a port_range through /ok; a missing range alone says to run /ok, which suggests one.

scripts/ports-blocklist lists well-known ports below 1025 as well as the popular defaults above it (3000, 4200, 5000, 5173, 5432, 6379, 8000, 8080, 8443, 9000, 9200, 27017 among them); the ESTATE_FILES row carries '# @decision: ports-leased-from-a-project-range' beside the EXECUTABLE_FILES row's.

A planner port-block copy that cannot be removed with git rm (untracked, uncommitted, or a link) is an estate-edits offer worded as a state file: 'the port reader an earlier ok-planner release materialized, which nothing reads now'. The removal uses remove_files(plan['removes'], root), the stop the sibling migrations use. The planner copy joins retired_scripts() whenever head_stamped finds the stamp, a link to a stamped file included, so a link becomes an offer.

The ephemeral refusal in amend compares the draft's port_range with the current file's, read through config_defects(target); resolve config compares it with the offer's keep (None when the current file does not parse, so any draft range is checked). ADMINISTRATION.md's amend refusal list and the config draft's resolve refusals name it (planning call i3, port-config call i11).

In true-up mode the core probes ports --help before it writes the ESTATE_FILES rows, so on a fresh project the block list lands after the probe; --help reads no block list, so the probe passes. Verified in a scratch project: the first true-up wrote bin/ports and bin/ports-blocklist; a tracked stamped bin/port-block with a caller filed retired-planner-port-block-caller-scripts-stack-start and stayed; with the caller gone it was removed with git rm; an untracked copy became estate-edits:.ok-planner/bin/port-block.

body: ports cleanup measures each container artifact's age against the docker daemon's own clock (docker info SystemTime), never the host clock, so the hour of grace subtracts two times from one clock (plumbline-coding rule 3.6); a lease's age uses the host clock its 'at' was written with.

ports cleanup dates an image by the later of its Created time and its Metadata.LastTagTime: a fully cached build tags an image whose Created time is old, and Created alone would let the cleanup untag a live run's fresh image.

ports cleanup counts a removal as done when docker answers 'no such image', 'no such volume' (case-insensitive), or 'network <name> not found': docker 29.6 words a missing volume 'get <name>: no such volume' and a missing network 'network <name> not found', not 'No such volume/network' as the notes quote. The same absence answer on a bulk inspect keeps the objects docker did return.

ports cleanup finds run tags from images (an exact run-tag tag, or a repository named <tag>- / <tag>_), and from the compose-project labels of volumes and networks; it does not list container labels, since a tag that has containers is never removed. It checks containers per tag with docker ps -a -q --filter label=com.docker.compose.project=<tag> for each lease it would free and again right before each tag's removals.

ports cleanup writes the registry once after the frees and prints the freed: lines then, and prints each removed: line right after that tag's removals, so a docker failure partway leaves the frees recorded and the output naming every tag already cleaned; the lock is held for the whole call (registry_lock, split out of transaction as a context manager both use).

compose-ports reports one violation per entry: its rule (patternKey compose-ports:<n>) is the lowest-numbered rule the entry breaks, and its message names every rule the entry breaks, joined with '; ', so one fix round covers an entry that is both undeclared and without a fallback (plumbline::checkComposePorts, ::composePortBreaks).

plumbline compose-ports reads the config leniently (ignore entries that are strings, folders only when well formed, via declaredFolders) and never refuses on a malformed config, so the core's port-range offer still reads compose files while a config offer is pending; it exits 1 only on a usage error, a missing target, or an internal error (plumbline::composeConfig). ignorePatterns(userConfig) is factored out of loadConfig so both share one builder; loadConfig's behavior is unchanged.

plumbline compose-ports prints every ports entry, including one that names no host port (variables [], port null); for a host port range or fallback range, port is the range's first port; host port 0 is not a port number. The reader strips a !override/!reset tag on ports:, reads only ports: keys directly under a service of the top-level services: key (deploy:, x- extension blocks, anchors, aliases, merge keys, extends, include are not read), and reads one-line flow sequences with scalar or {target, published} items.

admin/true-up::published_ports exits the core with 'true-up: plumbline compose-ports could not read the compose files (exit <n>): <detail>' on a non-zero exit, the shape config_defects uses for config-check; it returns [] where node is not on PATH. No caller yet: the port-range offer stage (port_range_offer) consumes it.

body: admin/true-up check-range relays the one-line answer of scripts/ports check-range (the range's size, each block-listed port it hits with what uses it, and the count left to lease) instead of the notes' three-line range:/listed:/leasable: form: scripts/ports is outside this stage's files and the core never re-reads the block list, so the core reformats nothing; refusals print as 'check-range: <ports' reason>' with exit 1.

admin/true-up::port_range_offer also stands where ports keeps the retired object form beside a declared port_range (draft converts ports and keeps the range, no suggestion run), and where the retired form names no port and nothing publishes one (draft removes ports, adds no range), so every config whose only defect is the retired form gets the converting offer the config item promises.

admin/true-up::port_range_offer lists a compose host-port variable that is not a NAME and leaves it out of the draft's ports (amend would refuse it through config-check); the NAME pattern is scripts/ports' PORT_NAME, loaded with carried_module, not a copy.

admin/true-up::offers withholds port-range whenever config_offers() returns any offer (its only kinds are config, config-key, citation-tags), and port_range_offer returns none while the lint config the core reads is not .ok-planner/config.json (a retired-layout config awaiting its move), so amend only ever targets the file the lint reads.

admin/true-up::ports_answer is the one reader of a scripts/ports read-only verb (suggest-range, check-range): exit 0 gives stdout, a last stderr line 'ports: <reason>' gives the refusal, anything else exits 'true-up: ports <verb> failed (exit n): <detail>'; range_refusal now uses it, so its internal-failure text changed from 'could not check the draft's port_range' to that line.

body: The story and decision globs and the falsifier concept path became named constants (STORY_FILES, DECISION_FILES, FALSIFIER_CONCEPT) that RETIRED_SECTIONS, the strips, diagnose, and the offers share, in place of the inline os.path.join lines inside strip_story_sections and strip_decision_proofs; checks/owned-paths' three needles now name the constant lines (plumbline-coding rule 6: one table for every reader).

After git rm of a removable falsifier concept, strip_story_sections recreates .ok-planner/design/concepts/ with os.makedirs(exist_ok=True): git rm prunes an emptied folder, so without it a project whose only concept was falsifier.md would show 'missing directory: .ok-planner/design/concepts' on the next diagnose and need a second true-up pass. The resolve path of the estate-edits offer keeps the sibling's prune; the next true-up recreates the folder.

I61: retired_section_files reads each story or decision as bytes, finds retired headings on a surrogateescape decode, and names a file as left only where it carries a retired heading and fails a strict UTF-8 decode, so a non-UTF-8 file with no retired section prints nothing. Diagnose prints the same left: line as a notice that does not change its exit status.

stripped matches a retired heading as the exact line '## <name>' anywhere in the file, including the first line, where the old regex required a preceding newline; the strip reads and writes bytes exactly (CRLF lines and trailing spaces survive), where read_owner's universal-newline read would have turned CRLF into LF.

The retired-sections offer's What reads '<path> holds the retired <## names> section(s), and it <state>; true-up strips a retired section itself only where git tracks the file unchanged and no symbolic link is involved, so it leaves this one to the owner.'; its resolve prints 'stripped: <path> — the retired <names> section(s)' and refuses a file that is itself a link with 'resolve: <path> is a symbolic link; nothing changed. Replace the link with the file it points at, or remove the link yourself, then run /ok again.'
